effective_tax_rate.what: The tax a company actually paid as a share of its profit before tax.
effective_tax_rate.read: Indian companies usually pay about 25%; ask why if the rate is far from that.
effective_tax_rate.why: An unusually low rate in one year can flatter profit and make growth from that year look slow later.
effective_tax_rate.formula: Tax expense ÷ profit before tax; blank when profit before tax is not positive.

roe.label: ROE
roe.what: How much profit a company makes for every ₹100 its shareholders have put in and left in the business.
roe.read: Compare with peers and the company's own past. Check debt too: borrowing can push ROE up.
roe.why: It shows whether owners' money is being used well; a business that earns more on each rupee can grow without asking for more.
roe.formula: The provider's return on equity: net profit ÷ shareholders' equity at the year end (not the average of two years). Blank when equity is zero or negative.

roce.label: ROCE
roce.what: Operating profit (EBIT) earned for every ₹100 of total capital used in the business, from both shareholders and lenders.
roce.read: A ROCE consistently above the cost of borrowing (roughly 10–12% in India) suggests the business creates value.
roce.why: Unlike ROE, it cannot be boosted by borrowing, so it is a fairer test of the business itself.
roce.formula: The provider's return on capital. Where the provider sends none, FinLit works out EBIT ÷ (total assets − current liabilities), with EBIT = profit before tax + finance costs. Not shown for banks and lenders.

roa.label: ROA
roa.what: Net profit earned for every ₹100 of assets the company owns.
roa.read: For banks, an ROA above about 1% is generally considered good.
roa.why: It is especially useful for banks and other lenders, whose assets are mostly loans.
roa.formula: Net profit ÷ total assets at the year end.

rota.label: Return on tangible assets
rota.what: Net profit as a share of physical and financial assets, leaving out goodwill and other intangibles.
rota.read: Use it alongside ROA when a company has bought many businesses.
rota.why: It removes the effect of past acquisitions, which inflate assets with goodwill.
rota.formula: The provider's net profit ÷ tangible assets (total assets less goodwill and other intangibles).

debt_to_equity.label: Debt / equity
debt_to_equity.what: Total borrowings divided by shareholders' equity: how much the company has borrowed for every rupee owners have put in. Some sources use total liabilities instead of borrowings.
debt_to_equity.read: Below 0.5 is generally comfortable for non-financial companies; banks are always much higher and need different measures.
debt_to_equity.why: More debt means fixed interest costs that must be paid even in bad years.
debt_to_equity.formula: Total borrowings ÷ shareholders' equity, as sent by the provider. Borrowings are loans, bonds and debentures (an NBFC's deposits count too). Blank when equity is zero or negative. Not shown for banks and lenders.

lt_debt_to_equity.label: Long-term debt / equity
lt_debt_to_equity.what: Only borrowings due after more than a year, divided by equity.
lt_debt_to_equity.read: A sharp rise usually means a big expansion or acquisition is being funded with loans.
lt_debt_to_equity.why: Long-term debt funds factories and projects; short-term debt funds daily operations.
lt_debt_to_equity.formula: Borrowings due after more than a year ÷ shareholders' equity, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

financial_leverage.label: Financial leverage
financial_leverage.what: Total assets divided by shareholders' equity.
financial_leverage.read: A value of 2.4 means owners fund about 42% of assets and liabilities fund the rest.
financial_leverage.why: It shows how much of the asset base is funded by owners versus others.
financial_leverage.formula: Total assets ÷ shareholders' equity, as sent by the provider. Blank when equity is zero or negative.

debt_to_assets.label: Debt / assets
debt_to_assets.what: Debt (or all liabilities) as a share of total assets. The equity ratio is the opposite: equity as a share of assets.
debt_to_assets.read: Rising ratios over several years mean the company is relying more on outside money.
debt_to_assets.why: They show how much of what the company owns is funded by others.
debt_to_assets.formula: Total borrowings ÷ total assets, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

debt_to_fcf.label: Debt / free cash flow
debt_to_fcf.what: Total debt divided by yearly free cash flow: how many years of spare cash it would take to repay all debt.
debt_to_fcf.read: Lower is better; a falling figure over years means the company is de-risking.
debt_to_fcf.why: It tests whether debt is affordable from real cash, not accounting profit.
debt_to_fcf.formula: Total borrowings ÷ free cash flow of the year, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

liabilities_to_assets.label: Liabilities / assets
liabilities_to_assets.what: Debt (or all liabilities) as a share of total assets. The equity ratio is the opposite: equity as a share of assets.
liabilities_to_assets.read: Rising ratios over several years mean the company is relying more on outside money.
liabilities_to_assets.why: They show how much of what the company owns is funded by others.
liabilities_to_assets.formula: Total liabilities ÷ total assets on the latest annual balance sheet. Not shown for banks and lenders.

current_ratio.label: Current ratio
current_ratio.what: Current assets divided by current liabilities: can the company pay bills due within a year from assets it will turn into cash within a year?
current_ratio.read: Around 1.2 to 2 is typical; well below 1 can mean a cash squeeze, though some businesses run safely that way.
current_ratio.why: It is a basic test of short-term safety.
current_ratio.formula: Current assets ÷ current liabilities, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

quick_ratio.label: Quick ratio
quick_ratio.what: Like the current ratio but leaving out inventory, which may be slow to sell.
quick_ratio.read: A quick ratio near or above 1 means short-term bills are covered without selling stock.
quick_ratio.why: It is a stricter test of whether bills can be paid quickly.
quick_ratio.formula: (Current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

interest_coverage.label: Interest coverage
interest_coverage.what: Operating profit (EBIT) divided by interest expense: how many times over the company can pay its interest.
interest_coverage.read: Below 1.5 is weak, above 3 is generally comfortable; FinLit flags 'weak interest cover' as a red flag.
interest_coverage.why: Low coverage means a small fall in profit could make interest hard to pay.
interest_coverage.formula: EBIT ÷ interest expense, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

asset_turnover.label: Asset turnover
asset_turnover.what: Revenue divided by average total assets: how many rupees of sales each rupee of assets produces.
asset_turnover.read: Retailers have high asset turnover; power companies have low. Compare within an industry.
asset_turnover.why: High turnover means assets are used intensively.
asset_turnover.formula: The provider's asset turnover. Where it sends none, FinLit uses revenue ÷ total assets at the year end (not the average of two years). Not shown for banks and lenders.

inventory_days.label: Inventory days
inventory_days.what: How many days, on average, goods sit in stock before being sold.
inventory_days.read: Rising inventory days can be an early sign of slowing demand.
inventory_days.why: Fewer days means less cash tied up and less risk of stock going obsolete.
inventory_days.formula: Inventory ÷ cost of goods sold × 365, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

debtor_days.label: Debtor days
debtor_days.what: How many days, on average, customers take to pay.
debtor_days.read: Compare with peers and with the company's own trend.
debtor_days.why: Slow collection ties up cash and can hide weak sales quality.
debtor_days.formula: Receivables ÷ revenue × 365, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

payable_days.label: Payable days
payable_days.what: How many days, on average, the company takes to pay its suppliers.
payable_days.read: Very long payable days can mean the company is short of cash.
payable_days.why: Paying later keeps cash in the business longer.
payable_days.formula: Payables ÷ cost of goods sold × 365, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

cash_conversion_cycle.label: Cash conversion cycle
cash_conversion_cycle.what: The number of days between paying for materials and collecting cash from customers.
cash_conversion_cycle.read: A cycle that lengthens year after year signals tightening cash.
cash_conversion_cycle.why: A short or negative cycle means suppliers effectively fund the business.
cash_conversion_cycle.formula: Inventory days + debtor days − payable days, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

revenue_cagr_3y.label: 3Y sales CAGR
revenue_cagr_3y.what: Average yearly growth in sales over the last 3 years.
revenue_cagr_3y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
revenue_cagr_3y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
revenue_cagr_3y.formula: (Sales this year ÷ sales 3 years ago)^(1 ÷ 3) − 1, on the Revenue line of FinLit's P&L (a lender: interest earned).

revenue_cagr_5y.label: 5Y sales CAGR
revenue_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in sales over the last 5 years.
revenue_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
revenue_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
revenue_cagr_5y.formula: (Sales this year ÷ sales 5 years ago)^(1 ÷ 5) − 1, on the Revenue line of FinLit's P&L (a lender: interest earned).

profit_cagr_3y.label: 3Y profit CAGR
profit_cagr_3y.what: Average yearly growth in net profit over the last 3 years.
profit_cagr_3y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
profit_cagr_3y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
profit_cagr_3y.formula: The provider's 3-year compound growth in net profit.

profit_cagr_5y.label: 5Y profit CAGR
profit_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in net profit over the last 5 years.
profit_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
profit_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
profit_cagr_5y.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in net profit.

eps_cagr_5y.label: 5Y EPS CAGR
eps_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in earnings per share over the last 5 years.
eps_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
eps_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
eps_cagr_5y.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in earnings per share.

ebitda_cagr_5y.label: 5Y EBITDA CAGR
ebitda_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in EBITDA over the last 5 years.
ebitda_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
ebitda_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
ebitda_cagr_5y.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in EBITDA.

book_value_cagr_5y.label: 5Y book value CAGR
book_value_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in book value over the last 5 years.
book_value_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
book_value_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
book_value_cagr_5y.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in book value (shareholders' equity).

cfo_cagr_3y.label: 3Y operating cash CAGR
cfo_cagr_3y.what: Average yearly growth in operating cash flow over the last 3 years.
cfo_cagr_3y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
cfo_cagr_3y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
cfo_cagr_3y.formula: The provider's 3-year compound growth in operating cash flow.

sales_cagr.label: Sales CAGR
sales_cagr.what: Average yearly growth in sales (up to 5 years).
sales_cagr.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
sales_cagr.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
sales_cagr.formula: (Sales this year ÷ sales N years ago)^(1 ÷ N) − 1 on FinLit's P&L, with N up to 5 years depending on how many years are held; the shown period says N.

profit_cagr.label: Profit CAGR
profit_cagr.what: Average yearly growth in net profit (up to 5 years).
profit_cagr.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
profit_cagr.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
profit_cagr.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in net profit; where it sends none, FinLit works it out from its own P&L over up to 5 years. The shown period says how many.

sales_growth_latest.label: Sales growth (latest year)
sales_growth_latest.what: Growth in sales over the latest year.
sales_growth_latest.read: Check both 3-year and 5-year rates. If they differ a lot, one of the start years was unusual.
sales_growth_latest.why: Profit growing faster than sales means margins are widening; slower means they are shrinking.
sales_growth_latest.formula: Sales this year ÷ sales last year − 1. For a company with only one annual result, the latest quarter against the same quarter a year earlier (the shown period says so).

profit_growth_latest.label: Profit growth (latest year)
profit_growth_latest.what: Growth in net profit over the latest year.
profit_growth_latest.read: Check both 3-year and 5-year rates. If they differ a lot, one of the start years was unusual.
profit_growth_latest.why: Profit growing faster than sales means margins are widening; slower means they are shrinking.
profit_growth_latest.formula: Net profit this year ÷ net profit last year − 1; blank when last year's profit was zero or a loss. For a company with only one annual result, the latest quarter against the same quarter a year earlier.

dividend_payout.label: Dividend payout
dividend_payout.what: The share of profit paid out as dividends.
dividend_payout.read: Above 100% means the company is paying more than it earns, which cannot last.
dividend_payout.why: Low payout keeps cash for growth; high payout returns more now but leaves less to reinvest.
dividend_payout.formula: Dividend per share declared for the year ÷ EPS of the same year; blank when EPS is not positive.

retention_ratio.label: Retention ratio
retention_ratio.what: The share of profit kept in the business rather than paid out.
retention_ratio.read: Retention only helps owners if the company earns a good return (ROE) on what it keeps.
retention_ratio.formula: Share of profit kept in the business, as sent by the provider (100% − payout).

cfo_to_pat.label: Cash conversion (CFO/PAT)
cfo_to_pat.what: Operating cash flow as a percentage of net profit. FinLit also shows free cash flow to profit.
cfo_to_pat.read: Around 80% or more over several years is healthy; FinLit flags 'profit not backed by cash' when it is weak.
cfo_to_pat.why: It tests whether reported profit is turning into real cash.
cfo_to_pat.formula: Operating cash flow ÷ net profit for the latest year that has both, as a percentage. Left blank when profit is zero or negative. Not shown for banks and lenders.

fcf_to_pat.label: FCF / PAT
fcf_to_pat.what: Free cash flow as a percentage of net profit: how much of the profit is left as spare cash after capital spending.
fcf_to_pat.read: Around 80% or more over several years is healthy; FinLit flags 'profit not backed by cash' when it is weak.
fcf_to_pat.why: It tests whether reported profit is turning into real cash.
fcf_to_pat.formula: Free cash flow ÷ net profit for the latest year that has both, as a percentage. Left blank when profit is zero or negative. Not shown for banks and lenders.

exceptional_share.label: One-off items / pre-tax profit
exceptional_share.what: How large the year's one-off gains or losses are against its pre-tax profit.
exceptional_share.read: Look at profit both with and without exceptional items before judging a quarter.
exceptional_share.formula: Exceptional items ÷ absolute profit before tax in the latest year.

rsi14.label: RSI (14)
rsi14.what: A 0–100 gauge of how strongly a stock has risen versus fallen over the last 14 days.
rsi14.read: Above 70 is usually called overbought, below 30 oversold. Strong trends can stay overbought or oversold for weeks.
rsi14.why: It flags when moves look stretched.
rsi14.formula: Wilder's RSI on 14 daily closes: 100 − 100 ÷ (1 + average gain ÷ average loss).

price.label: Share price
price.what: The LTP is the price of the most recent trade. The closing price is the official price at the end of the trading day, calculated by the exchange from the last half hour of trades.
price.read: During market hours (9:15 am to 3:30 pm on weekdays) prices move; after the close they stay fixed until the next session.
price.why: Returns, charts and most ratios use the closing price.
price.formula: Latest price in the quote data; when the market is closed, the last close.

enterprise_value.label: Enterprise value
enterprise_value.what: The value of the whole business to everyone with a claim on it: market cap plus debt, minus cash.
enterprise_value.read: Use EV-based ratios when comparing companies with very different debt levels.
enterprise_value.why: It is what a buyer would really pay, since they take on the debt and get the cash.
enterprise_value.formula: Market cap + borrowings − cash and cash equivalents from the latest annual balance sheet (₹ crore). Cash is the balance-sheet cash line only; investments are not subtracted. Not shown for banks and lenders.

revenue.label: Sales (revenue)
revenue.what: The money a company earns from selling its goods or services before any costs are taken out. Also called sales, turnover or the 'top line'.
revenue.read: Check whether growth comes from selling more or from charging more, and whether it lasts several years.
revenue.why: Growth in revenue is the starting point for growth in profit.
revenue.formula: Revenue from operations in the latest full financial year (a lender: interest earned), in ₹ crore.

net_profit.label: Net profit
net_profit.what: Profit left after every expense, interest and tax: the 'bottom line'. Often called PAT, profit after tax.
net_profit.read: Check whether net profit is backed by operating cash flow, and whether one-off items inflated it.
net_profit.why: It is the profit that belongs to shareholders and the base for EPS and P/E.
net_profit.formula: Profit attributable to the company's shareholders in the latest full year, in ₹ crore. Where profit from a discontinued business is material (a demerger gain), ratios and the screener use the continuing-operations profit.

total_assets.label: Total assets
total_assets.what: Everything the company owns, as shown on its balance sheet.
total_assets.read: Look at the mix: cash is safer than goodwill, and inventory that piles up can be a warning.
total_assets.why: Assets are what the business uses to earn money.
total_assets.formula: Total assets on the latest annual balance sheet, in ₹ crore.

book_value_ps.label: Book value per share
book_value_ps.what: Shareholders' equity divided by the number of shares.
book_value_ps.read: Growth in book value per share over years shows the company is building owners' wealth.
book_value_ps.why: It is the accounting value backing each share.
book_value_ps.formula: Shareholders' equity ÷ number of shares. The share count is the reported diluted count, or net profit ÷ EPS where it is not reported.

eps.label: Earnings per share
eps.what: The company's net profit divided by the number of shares: how much profit each share 'earns'.
eps.read: Compare EPS growth with profit growth; if EPS grows slower, new shares are diluting owners.
eps.why: EPS growth drives share prices over the long run, and it is the 'E' in P/E.
eps.formula: Reported EPS of the latest full year; scaled to continuing-operations profit when a discontinued business makes up a material part of profit.

ret_1m.label: 1-month return
ret_1m.what: The change in the share price over the last month.
ret_1m.read: 50% over five years is about 8.4% a year.
ret_1m.why: Returns over different periods can only be compared once annualised.
ret_1m.formula: Latest close ÷ the close one month earlier − 1 (price only, dividends excluded, not annualised); blank when there is no close within a week of that date.

ret_3m.label: 3-month return
ret_3m.what: The change in the share price over the last 3 months.
ret_3m.read: 50% over five years is about 8.4% a year.
ret_3m.why: Returns over different periods can only be compared once annualised.
ret_3m.formula: Latest close ÷ the close 3 months earlier − 1 (price only, dividends excluded, not annualised); blank when there is no close within a week of that date.

ret_6m.label: 6-month return
ret_6m.what: The change in the share price over the last 6 months.
ret_6m.read: 50% over five years is about 8.4% a year.
ret_6m.why: Returns over different periods can only be compared once annualised.
ret_6m.formula: Latest close ÷ the close 6 months earlier − 1 (price only, dividends excluded, not annualised); blank when there is no close within a week of that date.

ret_1y.label: 1-year return
ret_1y.what: The change in the share price over the last year.
ret_1y.read: 50% over five years is about 8.4% a year.
ret_1y.why: Returns over different periods can only be compared once annualised.
ret_1y.formula: Latest close ÷ the close one year earlier − 1 (price only, dividends excluded, not annualised); blank when there is no close within a week of that date.

ret_3y.label: 3-year return
ret_3y.what: The change in the share price over the last 3 years.
ret_3y.read: 50% over five years is about 8.4% a year.
ret_3y.why: Returns over different periods can only be compared once annualised.
ret_3y.formula: Latest close ÷ the close 3 years earlier − 1 (price only, dividends excluded, not annualised); blank when there is no close within a week of that date.

ret_5y.label: 5-year return
ret_5y.what: The change in the share price over the last 5 years.
ret_5y.read: 50% over five years is about 8.4% a year.
ret_5y.why: Returns over different periods can only be compared once annualised.
ret_5y.formula: Latest close ÷ the close 5 years earlier − 1 (price only, dividends excluded, not annualised); blank when there is no close within a week of that date.

ret_1d.label: 1-day change
ret_1d.read: 50% over five years is about 8.4% a year.
ret_1d.why: Returns over different periods can only be compared once annualised.
ret_1d.formula: Change in the latest price against the previous close.

ret_1y_total.label: 1-year total return
ret_1y_total.what: The full gain from an investment: price change plus dividends or interest received.
ret_1y_total.read: FinLit's total return table adds dividends to price change.
ret_1y_total.why: Price alone understates returns from dividend-paying stocks.
ret_1y_total.formula: Price change over one year plus adjusted dividends with an ex-date in that year, as a percentage of the starting close.

peg.label: PEG ratio
peg.what: The P/E ratio divided by the expected or recent EPS growth rate.
peg.read: As a rough guide, a PEG near 1 is often called fairly priced; it is only as good as the growth figure used.
peg.why: It adjusts P/E for growth: a high P/E may be fair for a fast grower.
peg.formula: P/E ÷ the 5-year compound growth rate of net profit (in %). FinLit uses profit growth, not EPS growth; shown only when both P/E and growth are positive.

earnings_yield.label: Earnings yield
earnings_yield.what: The inverse of P/E: yearly profit per share as a percentage of the share price.
earnings_yield.read: A P/E of 20 is an earnings yield of 5%; compare that with what a fixed deposit pays.
earnings_yield.why: It lets you compare a stock's earning power with interest rates on bonds or deposits.
earnings_yield.formula: 100 ÷ P/E; shown only when P/E is positive.

graham_value.label: Graham fair value
graham_value.what: A rough fair value per share from the investor Benjamin Graham's formula, using EPS and book value per share.
graham_value.read: 'Upside to Graham value' is how far the Graham number sits above the current price. It is meaningless for loss-making firms.
graham_value.why: It is a conservative cross-check for steady, profitable companies.
graham_value.formula: √(22.5 × EPS × book value per share); shown only when both are positive.

graham_upside.label: Upside to Graham value
graham_upside.what: How far the share price sits below (+) or above (−) the Graham number.
graham_upside.read: 'Upside to Graham value' is how far the Graham number sits above the current price. It is meaningless for loss-making firms.
graham_upside.why: It is a conservative cross-check for steady, profitable companies.
graham_upside.formula: (Graham fair value − share price) ÷ share price × 100. Positive means the price is below the Graham value.

ev_cfo.label: EV / CFO
ev_cfo.what: Enterprise value divided by revenue (EV/Sales) or by operating cash flow (EV/CFO).
ev_cfo.read: Use them alongside EV/EBITDA, not on their own.
ev_cfo.why: They extend the EV idea to companies with thin profits or lumpy earnings.
ev_cfo.formula: Enterprise value ÷ operating cash flow of the latest year; blank when operating cash flow is not positive. Not shown for banks and lenders.

ev_sales.label: EV / Sales
ev_sales.what: Enterprise value divided by revenue (EV/Sales) or by operating cash flow (EV/CFO).
ev_sales.read: Use them alongside EV/EBITDA, not on their own.
ev_sales.why: They extend the EV idea to companies with thin profits or lumpy earnings.
ev_sales.formula: Enterprise value ÷ sales of the latest year. Not shown for banks and lenders.

price_cfo.label: Price / CFO
price_cfo.what: Market cap divided by yearly operating cash flow (P/CFO) or by free cash flow (P/FCF).
price_cfo.read: If P/FCF is far higher than P/E, profits are not turning into spare cash.
price_cfo.why: Cash is harder to dress up than profit, so these ratios can be more reliable than P/E.
price_cfo.formula: Market cap ÷ operating cash flow of the latest year; blank when operating cash flow is not positive. Not shown for banks and lenders.

fcf_yield.label: FCF yield
fcf_yield.what: Free cash flow as a percentage of market cap: the spare cash the business generates for each ₹100 of its market value.
fcf_yield.read: A higher FCF yield means more spare cash for each ₹100 of market value, if the cash flow is steady.
fcf_yield.why: It shows how much cash an owner of the whole company would receive each year.
fcf_yield.formula: Free cash flow of the latest year ÷ market cap × 100. Not shown for banks and lenders.

sales_ps.label: Sales per share
sales_ps.what: Company totals divided by the number of shares: sales per share, cash per share, net cash per share, free cash flow per share.
sales_ps.read: Net cash per share above zero means the company has more cash than debt.
sales_ps.why: They let you compare a company's numbers directly with its share price.
sales_ps.formula: Sales of the latest year ÷ number of shares.

cash_ps.label: Cash per share
cash_ps.what: Company totals divided by the number of shares: sales per share, cash per share, net cash per share, free cash flow per share.
cash_ps.read: Net cash per share above zero means the company has more cash than debt.
cash_ps.why: They let you compare a company's numbers directly with its share price.
cash_ps.formula: Cash and cash equivalents ÷ number of shares. Not shown for banks and lenders.

net_cash_ps.label: Net cash per share
net_cash_ps.what: Company totals divided by the number of shares: sales per share, cash per share, net cash per share, free cash flow per share.
net_cash_ps.read: Net cash per share above zero means the company has more cash than debt.
net_cash_ps.why: They let you compare a company's numbers directly with its share price.
net_cash_ps.formula: (Cash and cash equivalents − borrowings) ÷ number of shares. Negative means net debt. Investments are not counted. Not shown for banks and lenders.

fcf_ps.label: FCF per share
fcf_ps.what: Company totals divided by the number of shares: sales per share, cash per share, net cash per share, free cash flow per share.
fcf_ps.read: Net cash per share above zero means the company has more cash than debt.
fcf_ps.why: They let you compare a company's numbers directly with its share price.
fcf_ps.formula: Free cash flow of the latest year ÷ number of shares. Not shown for banks and lenders.

pe_median_5y.label: Median P/E (5Y)
pe_median_5y.what: The middle value when numbers are lined up in order; half are above it and half below.
pe_median_5y.read: FinLit compares ratios with their 5-year or 8-year median, and companies with the sector median.
pe_median_5y.why: It is less distorted by extreme values than the average.
pe_median_5y.formula: The middle value of the last five yearly P/E readings (needs at least three).

pe_vs_median_5y.label: P/E vs own 5Y median
pe_vs_median_5y.what: How far today's P/E sits above (+) or below (−) its own median of the last five years.
pe_vs_median_5y.read: Trading below its own 5-year median P/E can mean the shares are priced lower than usual, or that growth has slowed. Check why.
pe_vs_median_5y.why: A ratio means little alone; context shows whether it is high or low.

pb_vs_median_5y.label: P/B vs own 5Y median
pb_vs_median_5y.what: How far today's P/B sits above (+) or below (−) its own median of the last five years.
pb_vs_median_5y.read: Trading below its own 5-year median P/E can mean the shares are priced lower than usual, or that growth has slowed. Check why.
pb_vs_median_5y.why: A ratio means little alone; context shows whether it is high or low.

pe_vs_sector.label: P/E vs sector median
pe_vs_sector.what: How far the P/E sits above (+) or below (−) the median of its sector.
pe_vs_sector.read: Trading below its own 5-year median P/E can mean the shares are priced lower than usual, or that growth has slowed. Check why.
pe_vs_sector.why: A ratio means little alone; context shows whether it is high or low.
pe_vs_sector.formula: (P/E − median P/E of the company's sector) ÷ sector median × 100.

pb_vs_sector.label: P/B vs sector median
pb_vs_sector.what: How far the P/B sits above (+) or below (−) the median of its sector.
pb_vs_sector.read: Trading below its own 5-year median P/E can mean the shares are priced lower than usual, or that growth has slowed. Check why.
pb_vs_sector.why: A ratio means little alone; context shows whether it is high or low.
pb_vs_sector.formula: (P/B − median P/B of the company's sector) ÷ sector median × 100.

price_to_tangible.label: Market cap to total assets
price_to_tangible.what: What the stock market pays for each rupee of assets the company owns.
price_to_tangible.read: A P/B below 1 means the market values the company below its book value; find out why before calling it cheap.
price_to_tangible.why: Most useful for banks, insurers and asset-heavy companies, whose assets are close to their real value.
price_to_tangible.formula: Market cap ÷ total assets of the latest year (assets, not net assets, so it differs from P/B).

pe_avg_3y.label: P/E, 3Y average
pe_avg_3y.what: The average P/E over the last three years.
pe_avg_3y.read: Compare P/E with the company's own history and its industry. A low P/E can mean cheap, or it can mean the market expects profits to fall.
pe_avg_3y.why: It is the quickest way to judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its profits.
pe_avg_3y.formula: Average of the last three yearly P/E readings (needs at least three readings).

pe_avg_5y.label: P/E, 5Y average
pe_avg_5y.what: The average P/E over the last five years.
pe_avg_5y.read: Compare P/E with the company's own history and its industry. A low P/E can mean cheap, or it can mean the market expects profits to fall.
pe_avg_5y.why: It is the quickest way to judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its profits.
pe_avg_5y.formula: Average of the last five yearly P/E readings (needs at least three readings).

pe_avg_7y.label: P/E, 7Y average
pe_avg_7y.what: The average P/E over the last seven years.
pe_avg_7y.read: Compare P/E with the company's own history and its industry. A low P/E can mean cheap, or it can mean the market expects profits to fall.
pe_avg_7y.why: It is the quickest way to judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its profits.
pe_avg_7y.formula: Average of the last seven yearly P/E readings (needs at least three readings).

pb_avg_3y.label: P/B, 3Y average
pb_avg_3y.what: The average P/B over the last three years.
pb_avg_3y.read: A P/B below 1 means the market values the company below its book value; find out why before calling it cheap.
pb_avg_3y.why: Most useful for banks, insurers and asset-heavy companies, whose assets are close to their real value.
pb_avg_3y.formula: Average of the last three yearly P/B readings (needs at least three readings).

pb_avg_5y.label: P/B, 5Y average
pb_avg_5y.what: The average P/B over the last five years.
pb_avg_5y.read: A P/B below 1 means the market values the company below its book value; find out why before calling it cheap.
pb_avg_5y.why: Most useful for banks, insurers and asset-heavy companies, whose assets are close to their real value.
pb_avg_5y.formula: Average of the last five yearly P/B readings (needs at least three readings).

pb_avg_7y.label: P/B, 7Y average
pb_avg_7y.what: The average P/B over the last seven years.
pb_avg_7y.read: A P/B below 1 means the market values the company below its book value; find out why before calling it cheap.
pb_avg_7y.why: Most useful for banks, insurers and asset-heavy companies, whose assets are close to their real value.
pb_avg_7y.formula: Average of the last seven yearly P/B readings (needs at least three readings).

ps_avg_3y.label: P/S, 3Y average
ps_avg_3y.what: The average P/S over the last three years.
ps_avg_3y.read: Compare only within an industry; high-margin businesses naturally trade at higher P/S.
ps_avg_3y.why: Useful for young or loss-making companies that have no profit to put in a P/E.
ps_avg_3y.formula: Average of the last three yearly P/S readings (needs at least three readings).

ps_avg_5y.label: P/S, 5Y average
ps_avg_5y.what: The average P/S over the last five years.
ps_avg_5y.read: Compare only within an industry; high-margin businesses naturally trade at higher P/S.
ps_avg_5y.why: Useful for young or loss-making companies that have no profit to put in a P/E.
ps_avg_5y.formula: Average of the last five yearly P/S readings (needs at least three readings).

ps_avg_7y.label: P/S, 7Y average
ps_avg_7y.what: The average P/S over the last seven years.
ps_avg_7y.read: Compare only within an industry; high-margin businesses naturally trade at higher P/S.
ps_avg_7y.why: Useful for young or loss-making companies that have no profit to put in a P/E.
ps_avg_7y.formula: Average of the last seven yearly P/S readings (needs at least three readings).

tax_rate.label: Effective tax rate
tax_rate.what: The tax a company actually paid as a share of its profit before tax.
tax_rate.read: Indian companies usually pay about 25%; ask why if the rate is far from that.
tax_rate.why: An unusually low rate in one year can flatter profit and make growth from that year look slow later.
tax_rate.formula: Tax expense ÷ profit before tax; blank when profit before tax is not positive.

roe_3y.label: ROE, 3-year average
roe_3y.what: Average return on equity over the last three years.
roe_3y.read: Compare with peers and the company's own past. Check debt too: borrowing can push ROE up.
roe_3y.why: It shows whether owners' money is being used well; a business that earns more on each rupee can grow without asking for more.
roe_3y.formula: Average of the last three yearly ROE readings.

roce_3y.label: ROCE, 3-year average
roce_3y.what: Average return on capital employed over the last three years.
roce_3y.read: A ROCE consistently above the cost of borrowing (roughly 10–12% in India) suggests the business creates value.
roce_3y.why: Unlike ROE, it cannot be boosted by borrowing, so it is a fairer test of the business itself.
roce_3y.formula: Average of the last three yearly ROCE readings.

opm_3y.label: Operating margin, 3-year average
opm_3y.what: Average operating margin over the last three years.
opm_3y.read: A margin rising steadily over several years usually means growing efficiency or pricing power.
opm_3y.why: It shows how efficiently the core business runs.
opm_3y.formula: Average of the last three yearly operating profit ÷ sales figures.

opm_change.label: Operating margin change (1 year)
opm_change.what: Percentage points the operating margin moved in the latest year.
opm_change.read: A margin rising steadily over several years usually means growing efficiency or pricing power.
opm_change.why: It shows how efficiently the core business runs.
opm_change.formula: Operating profit ÷ sales this year minus the same figure last year, in percentage points.

sales_growth.label: Sales growth (latest year)
sales_growth.what: How much sales grew in the latest year.
sales_growth.read: Check both 3-year and 5-year rates. If they differ a lot, one of the start years was unusual.
sales_growth.why: Profit growing faster than sales means margins are widening; slower means they are shrinking.
sales_growth.formula: Sales this year ÷ sales last year − 1.

profit_growth.label: Profit growth (latest year)
profit_growth.what: How much net profit grew in the latest year.
profit_growth.read: Check both 3-year and 5-year rates. If they differ a lot, one of the start years was unusual.
profit_growth.why: Profit growing faster than sales means margins are widening; slower means they are shrinking.
profit_growth.formula: Net profit this year ÷ net profit last year − 1; blank when last year's profit was zero or a loss.

sales_cagr_3y.label: Sales growth, 3 years a year
sales_cagr_3y.what: Average yearly growth in sales over the last 3 years.
sales_cagr_3y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
sales_cagr_3y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.

sales_cagr_5y.label: Sales growth, 5 years a year
sales_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in sales over the last 5 years.
sales_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
sales_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.

bv_cagr_5y.label: Book value growth, 5 years a year
bv_cagr_5y.what: Average yearly growth in book value over the last 5 years.
bv_cagr_5y.read: CAGR depends heavily on the start year: growth measured from a bad year looks better than it is.
bv_cagr_5y.why: It smooths out ups and downs so different periods and companies can be compared.
bv_cagr_5y.formula: The provider's 5-year compound growth in book value.

dps_cagr.label: Dividend growth (yearly)
dps_cagr.what: Average yearly growth in the dividend per share.
dps_cagr.read: Compare DPS over many years, adjusted for splits and bonuses, to see if payouts are growing.
dps_cagr.why: It is the cash you receive for each share you own.
dps_cagr.formula: Compound yearly growth in dividend per share, from the first year with a dividend in the last six years to the latest year; blank when the latest year has no dividend.

years_profit_up.label: Years of rising profit (last 5)
years_profit_up.what: In how many of the last five years net profit rose.
years_profit_up.read: FinLit's screener has filters for years and quarters of rising sales and profit.
years_profit_up.why: Steady growth is easier to trust and usually earns a higher valuation than lumpy growth.
years_profit_up.formula: Number of the last five years in which net profit was higher than the year before.

q_revenue.label: Latest quarter sales
q_revenue.what: Sales in the most recent quarter.
q_revenue.read: Compare a quarter with the same quarter a year earlier, because many businesses are seasonal.
q_revenue.why: They are the most frequent official update on how a business is doing.
q_revenue.formula: Revenue of the most recent quarter in the quarterly P&L, in ₹ crore.

q_net_profit.label: Latest quarter profit
q_net_profit.what: Net profit in the most recent quarter.
q_net_profit.read: Compare a quarter with the same quarter a year earlier, because many businesses are seasonal.
q_net_profit.why: They are the most frequent official update on how a business is doing.
q_net_profit.formula: Net profit of the most recent quarter, in ₹ crore.

q_operating_profit.label: Latest quarter operating profit
q_operating_profit.what: Operating profit in the most recent quarter.
q_operating_profit.read: Compare operating profit growth with revenue growth to see whether the business is becoming more or less efficient.
q_operating_profit.why: It shows how much the business itself earns, separate from how it is financed.
q_operating_profit.formula: Operating profit of the most recent quarter: revenue minus operating costs, before depreciation, interest and other income.

q_eps.label: Latest quarter EPS
q_eps.what: Earnings per share in the most recent quarter.
q_eps.read: Compare EPS growth with profit growth; if EPS grows slower, new shares are diluting owners.
q_eps.why: EPS growth drives share prices over the long run, and it is the 'E' in P/E.
q_eps.formula: Reported earnings per share of the most recent quarter.

q_sales_yoy.label: Sales growth vs same quarter last year
q_sales_yoy.what: Latest quarter's sales against the same quarter a year ago.
q_sales_yoy.read: Use YoY for quarterly results; use QoQ to spot turning points.
q_sales_yoy.why: It removes seasonal effects, like festive-season sales.
q_sales_yoy.formula: Quarter sales ÷ sales of the same quarter a year earlier − 1; blank when the earlier figure is zero or negative.

q_profit_yoy.label: Profit growth vs same quarter last year
q_profit_yoy.what: Latest quarter's net profit against the same quarter a year ago.
q_profit_yoy.read: Use YoY for quarterly results; use QoQ to spot turning points.
q_profit_yoy.why: It removes seasonal effects, like festive-season sales.
q_profit_yoy.formula: Quarter net profit ÷ net profit of the same quarter a year earlier − 1; blank when the earlier profit is zero or a loss.

q_sales_qoq.label: Sales growth vs previous quarter
q_sales_qoq.what: Latest quarter's sales against the quarter before.
q_sales_qoq.read: A strong QoQ jump in a seasonal business may just be the festive quarter.
q_sales_qoq.why: It shows the latest direction, but it is affected by seasons.
q_sales_qoq.formula: Quarter sales ÷ sales of the quarter before − 1.

q_profit_qoq.label: Profit growth vs previous quarter
q_profit_qoq.what: Latest quarter's net profit against the quarter before.
q_profit_qoq.read: A strong QoQ jump in a seasonal business may just be the festive quarter.
q_profit_qoq.why: It shows the latest direction, but it is affected by seasons.
q_profit_qoq.formula: Quarter net profit ÷ net profit of the quarter before − 1; blank when the earlier profit is zero or a loss.

q_opm.label: Latest quarter operating margin
q_opm.what: Operating margin in the most recent quarter.
q_opm.read: A margin rising steadily over several years usually means growing efficiency or pricing power.
q_opm.why: It shows how efficiently the core business runs.
q_opm.formula: Operating profit ÷ sales of the quarter.

q_npm.label: Latest quarter net margin
q_npm.what: Net margin in the most recent quarter.
q_npm.read: A net margin of 7.5% means ₹7.50 of profit for every ₹100 of sales.
q_npm.why: It shows how much of each ₹100 of sales the shareholders keep.
q_npm.formula: Net profit ÷ sales of the quarter.

ttm_revenue.label: Sales, last 12 months
ttm_revenue.what: Sales over the last four reported quarters.
ttm_revenue.read: P/E and many ratios on FinLit use TTM profit; a ratio marked FY uses the last full year instead.
ttm_revenue.why: It gives the most up-to-date yearly figure.
ttm_revenue.formula: Sum of the last four quarters' revenue.

ttm_net_profit.label: Profit, last 12 months
ttm_net_profit.what: Net profit over the last four reported quarters.
ttm_net_profit.read: P/E and many ratios on FinLit use TTM profit; a ratio marked FY uses the last full year instead.
ttm_net_profit.why: It gives the most up-to-date yearly figure.
ttm_net_profit.formula: Sum of the last four quarters' net profit.

ttm_eps.label: EPS, last 12 months
ttm_eps.what: Earnings per share over the last four reported quarters.
ttm_eps.read: P/E and many ratios on FinLit use TTM profit; a ratio marked FY uses the last full year instead.
ttm_eps.why: It gives the most up-to-date yearly figure.
ttm_eps.formula: Sum of the last four quarters' earnings per share.

q_sales_up.label: Quarters of rising sales (last 4, year on year)
q_sales_up.what: In how many of the last four quarters sales were higher than a year before.
q_sales_up.read: FinLit's screener has filters for years and quarters of rising sales and profit.
q_sales_up.why: Steady growth is easier to trust and usually earns a higher valuation than lumpy growth.
q_sales_up.formula: Number of the last four quarters whose sales beat the same quarter a year earlier.

q_profit_up.label: Quarters of rising profit (last 4, year on year)
q_profit_up.what: In how many of the last four quarters net profit was higher than a year before.
q_profit_up.read: FinLit's screener has filters for years and quarters of rising sales and profit.
q_profit_up.why: Steady growth is easier to trust and usually earns a higher valuation than lumpy growth.
q_profit_up.formula: Number of the last four quarters whose net profit beat the same quarter a year earlier.

net_debt.label: Net debt
net_debt.what: Total debt minus cash and equivalents. A negative figure means net cash.
net_debt.read: Net debt to EBITDA below about 2 is generally considered comfortable for most industries.
net_debt.why: It shows the real debt burden after using available cash.
net_debt.formula: Borrowings − cash and cash equivalents from the latest annual balance sheet (₹ crore). Investments are not subtracted. Negative means net cash. Not shown for banks and lenders.

net_debt_to_equity.label: Net debt to equity
net_debt_to_equity.what: Net debt for every rupee of shareholders' equity.
net_debt_to_equity.read: Net debt to EBITDA below about 2 is generally considered comfortable for most industries.
net_debt_to_equity.why: It shows the real debt burden after using available cash.
net_debt_to_equity.formula: Net debt ÷ shareholders' equity; blank when equity is zero or negative. Not shown for banks and lenders.

net_debt_to_ebitda.label: Net debt to EBITDA
net_debt_to_ebitda.what: Net debt divided by yearly EBITDA: roughly how many years of operating profit it would take to repay the debt.
net_debt_to_ebitda.read: Above 3 to 4 starts to look stretched for most businesses.
net_debt_to_ebitda.why: Lenders and rating agencies watch it closely.
net_debt_to_ebitda.formula: Net debt ÷ operating profit of the latest year (revenue minus operating costs, before depreciation and interest, excluding other income); blank when operating profit is not positive. Not shown for banks and lenders.

borrowings.label: Total borrowings
borrowings.what: All loans, bonds and debentures the company has taken, short and long term.
borrowings.read: Track debt alongside cash: rising debt with falling cash is a warning sign.
borrowings.why: Debt must be repaid or refinanced on time, whatever happens.
borrowings.formula: Bank loans, bonds, debentures and subordinated debt on the latest annual balance sheet (an NBFC's deposits count too), in ₹ crore.

cash.label: Cash and equivalents
cash.what: Money in the bank and very short-term, very safe investments that can be turned into cash at once.
cash.read: Compare cash with debt to get net debt.
cash.why: Cash gives a company room to survive bad times and invest when others cannot.
cash.formula: The cash and cash equivalents line of the latest annual balance sheet, in ₹ crore. Not shown for banks and lenders.

cash_to_debt.label: Cash to debt
cash_to_debt.what: Cash held for each rupee of borrowings.
cash_to_debt.read: Compare cash with debt to get net debt.
cash_to_debt.why: Cash gives a company room to survive bad times and invest when others cannot.
cash_to_debt.formula: Cash and cash equivalents ÷ borrowings. Not shown for banks and lenders.

fcf.label: Free cash flow
fcf.what: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditure: the spare cash left after keeping and growing the business.
fcf.read: A company with growing profit but negative FCF for years is consuming cash to grow.
fcf.why: FCF pays dividends, buybacks and debt repayment.
fcf.formula: Operating cash flow − capital expenditure for the latest year, in ₹ crore. Capital expenditure is the purchase of property, plant, equipment and intangibles in the cash-flow statement. Not shown for banks and lenders.

cfo.label: Operating cash flow
cfo.what: Cash generated by the main business in a period, after paying suppliers, staff and taxes.
cfo.read: Operating cash flow consistently below net profit needs explaining.
cfo.why: It is the clearest sign that a business really earns money.
cfo.formula: Cash flow from operating activities in the latest annual cash-flow statement, in ₹ crore. Not shown for banks and lenders.

current_assets.label: Current assets
current_assets.what: Assets the company expects to turn into cash within a year: cash, inventory and money owed by customers.
current_assets.read: Compare working capital with sales over several years; a sharp rise needs an explanation.
current_assets.why: Too little can mean trouble paying bills; too much means cash is stuck in stock and unpaid invoices.
current_assets.formula: Current assets on the annual balance sheet, in ₹ crore.

cash_to_current_liab.label: Cash to current liabilities
cash_to_current_liab.what: Cash held for each rupee of bills due within a year.
cash_to_current_liab.read: Check average daily traded value when researching small companies.
cash_to_current_liab.why: An illiquid stock can be hard to sell at a fair price when you need to.
cash_to_current_liab.formula: Cash and cash equivalents ÷ current liabilities. Not shown for banks and lenders.

working_capital.label: Working capital
working_capital.what: The money tied up in day-to-day operations: short-term assets (cash, inventory, receivables) minus short-term liabilities (payables, short-term debt).
working_capital.read: Compare working capital with sales over several years; a sharp rise needs an explanation.
working_capital.why: Too little can mean trouble paying bills; too much means cash is stuck in stock and unpaid invoices.
working_capital.formula: Current assets − current liabilities on the latest annual balance sheet, in ₹ crore. Not shown for banks and lenders.

working_capital_to_sales.label: Working capital to sales
working_capital_to_sales.what: Money tied up in day-to-day running, as a share of sales.
working_capital_to_sales.read: Compare working capital with sales over several years; a sharp rise needs an explanation.
working_capital_to_sales.why: Too little can mean trouble paying bills; too much means cash is stuck in stock and unpaid invoices.
working_capital_to_sales.formula: Working capital ÷ sales of the latest year × 100. Not shown for banks and lenders.

equity_ratio.label: Equity ratio
equity_ratio.what: The share of assets funded by owners' money rather than by others.
equity_ratio.read: Rising ratios over several years mean the company is relying more on outside money.
equity_ratio.why: They show how much of what the company owns is funded by others.

equity.label: Shareholders' equity
equity.what: What would be left for shareholders if the company sold all its assets and paid all its liabilities: the owners' stake. The word also means shares in general.
equity.read: Steady growth in equity alongside low debt is a sign of a sound business.
equity.why: Equity grows when profits are kept in the business and shrinks with losses.
equity.formula: Equity attributable to the company's own shareholders on the latest annual balance sheet (a bank: share capital plus reserves), in ₹ crore.

fixed_asset_turnover.label: Fixed asset turnover
fixed_asset_turnover.what: Revenue divided by fixed assets such as plant and machinery.
fixed_asset_turnover.read: A falling figure after a big expansion may just mean new capacity is still ramping up.
fixed_asset_turnover.why: It shows how well factories and equipment are being used.
fixed_asset_turnover.formula: Sales of the latest year ÷ fixed assets (property, plant and equipment) at the year end. Not shown for banks and lenders.

cash_cycle.label: Cash conversion cycle
cash_cycle.what: The number of days between paying for materials and collecting cash from customers.
cash_cycle.read: A cycle that lengthens year after year signals tightening cash.
cash_cycle.why: A short or negative cycle means suppliers effectively fund the business.
cash_cycle.formula: Inventory days + debtor days − payable days, as sent by the provider. Not shown for banks and lenders.

capex_to_sales.label: Capital spending to sales
capex_to_sales.what: Capital spending as a share of revenue or of operating cash flow.
capex_to_sales.read: Asset-light businesses need little capex and usually produce more free cash.
capex_to_sales.why: It shows how much the business must reinvest just to grow.
capex_to_sales.formula: Capital expenditure ÷ sales of the latest year × 100. Not shown for banks and lenders.

capex_to_cfo.label: Capital spending to operating cash
capex_to_cfo.what: Capital spending as a share of revenue or of operating cash flow.
capex_to_cfo.read: Asset-light businesses need little capex and usually produce more free cash.
capex_to_cfo.why: It shows how much the business must reinvest just to grow.
capex_to_cfo.formula: Capital expenditure ÷ operating cash flow of the latest year × 100; blank when operating cash flow is not positive. Not shown for banks and lenders.

sales_per_employee.label: Sales per employee
sales_per_employee.what: Revenue or net profit divided by the number of employees.
sales_per_employee.read: Useful within an industry, such as comparing IT services firms; meaningless across very different industries.
sales_per_employee.formula: Sales of the latest year ÷ number of employees in the company profile, in ₹ crore per person.

profit_per_employee.label: Profit per employee
profit_per_employee.what: Revenue or net profit divided by the number of employees.
profit_per_employee.read: Useful within an industry, such as comparing IT services firms; meaningless across very different industries.
profit_per_employee.formula: Net profit of the latest year ÷ number of employees in the company profile, in ₹ crore per person.

employees.label: Employees
employees.what: The number of people the company reports as employees.
employees.read: Useful within an industry, such as comparing IT services firms; meaningless across very different industries.

own_promoters.label: Promoter holding
own_promoters.what: The share of the company held by its promoters.
own_promoters.read: A rising pledged share is a classic warning sign.
own_promoters.why: If the share price falls, lenders can sell pledged shares, pushing the price down further.
own_promoters.formula: Share of the company's shares held by this group in the latest quarterly shareholding pattern.

own_fii.label: Foreign institutions
own_fii.what: The share of the company held by foreign institutional investors.
own_fii.read: Steady FII selling in a stock can weigh on its price for a while.
own_fii.why: Their flows move large-company prices and the market overall.
own_fii.formula: Share of the company's shares held by this group in the latest quarterly shareholding pattern.

own_dii.label: Domestic institutions
own_dii.what: The share of the company held by domestic institutions.
own_dii.read: Rising DII holding often reflects growing mutual-fund interest.
own_dii.why: Monthly SIP money has made DIIs a steady force in Indian markets.
own_dii.formula: Share of the company's shares held by this group in the latest quarterly shareholding pattern.

own_public.label: Public holding
own_public.what: The share of the company held by the public.
own_public.read: Compare the retail trend with institutional trends.
own_public.why: A rising retail share with falling institutional holding can mean professionals are selling to individuals.
own_public.formula: Share of the company's shares held by this group in the latest quarterly shareholding pattern.

own_government.label: Government holding
own_government.what: The share of the company held by the government.
own_government.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_government.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_government.formula: Share of the company's shares held by this group in the latest quarterly shareholding pattern.

own_institutions.label: All institutions
own_institutions.what: The combined share held by foreign and domestic institutions.
own_institutions.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_institutions.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_institutions.formula: Foreign plus domestic institutional holding in the latest shareholding pattern.

own_promoters_chg_1y.label: Promoter holding change (1 year)
own_promoters_chg_1y.what: Percentage points promoters added (+) or cut (−) in the last year.
own_promoters_chg_1y.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_promoters_chg_1y.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_promoters_chg_1y.formula: Holding of promoters in the latest shareholding pattern minus their holding a year earlier, in percentage points.

own_fii_chg_1y.label: Foreign institutions change (1 year)
own_fii_chg_1y.what: Percentage points foreign institutions added (+) or cut (−) in the last year.
own_fii_chg_1y.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_fii_chg_1y.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_fii_chg_1y.formula: Holding of foreign institutions in the latest shareholding pattern minus their holding a year earlier, in percentage points.

own_dii_chg_1y.label: Domestic institutions change (1 year)
own_dii_chg_1y.what: Percentage points domestic institutions added (+) or cut (−) in the last year.
own_dii_chg_1y.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_dii_chg_1y.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_dii_chg_1y.formula: Holding of domestic institutions in the latest shareholding pattern minus their holding a year earlier, in percentage points.

own_public_chg_1y.label: Public holding change (1 year)
own_public_chg_1y.what: Percentage points the public added (+) or cut (−) in the last year.
own_public_chg_1y.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_public_chg_1y.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_public_chg_1y.formula: Holding of the public in the latest shareholding pattern minus their holding a year earlier, in percentage points.

own_promoters_chg_1q.label: Promoter holding change (last quarter)
own_promoters_chg_1q.what: Percentage points promoters added (+) or cut (−) in the last quarter.
own_promoters_chg_1q.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_promoters_chg_1q.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_promoters_chg_1q.formula: Holding of promoters in the latest shareholding pattern minus their holding in the quarter before, in percentage points.

own_fii_chg_1q.label: Foreign institutions change (last quarter)
own_fii_chg_1q.what: Percentage points foreign institutions added (+) or cut (−) in the last quarter.
own_fii_chg_1q.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_fii_chg_1q.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_fii_chg_1q.formula: Holding of foreign institutions in the latest shareholding pattern minus their holding in the quarter before, in percentage points.

own_dii_chg_1q.label: Domestic institutions change (last quarter)
own_dii_chg_1q.what: Percentage points domestic institutions added (+) or cut (−) in the last quarter.
own_dii_chg_1q.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_dii_chg_1q.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_dii_chg_1q.formula: Holding of domestic institutions in the latest shareholding pattern minus their holding in the quarter before, in percentage points.

own_inst_chg_1y.label: Institutions change (1 year)
own_inst_chg_1y.what: Percentage points all institutions added (+) or cut (−) in a year.
own_inst_chg_1y.read: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.
own_inst_chg_1y.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
own_inst_chg_1y.formula: Change in foreign plus domestic institutional holding over a year, in percentage points.

div_ttm.label: Dividend per share (last 12 months)
div_ttm.what: The total dividend paid in a year divided by the number of shares.
div_ttm.read: Compare DPS over many years, adjusted for splits and bonuses, to see if payouts are growing.
div_ttm.why: It is the cash you receive for each share you own.
div_ttm.formula: Sum of split- and bonus-adjusted dividends per share with an ex-date in the last 365 days.

div_last_days.label: Days since last dividend
div_last_days.what: How long ago the last dividend went ex.
div_last_days.read: Note ex-dates for stocks you plan to buy or sell.
div_last_days.why: Buying just before the ex-date to 'collect' a dividend rarely works because the price adjusts.
div_last_days.formula: Days from the most recent past ex-dividend date to today.

div_years.label: Years of dividends (last 6)
div_years.what: In how many of the last six years a dividend was declared.
div_years.read: A dividend cut is often a warning about the business; steady increases suggest confidence.
div_years.why: Dividends give a return without selling shares.
div_years.formula: Number of the last six financial years in which a dividend was declared.

div_paying.label: Pays a dividend
div_paying.what: Whether the company declared a dividend in the last 12 months.
div_paying.read: A dividend cut is often a warning about the business; steady increases suggest confidence.
div_paying.why: Dividends give a return without selling shares.
div_paying.formula: Yes (1) when a dividend with an ex-date in the last 12 months exists, otherwise no (0).

bonus_3y.label: Bonus issue in last 3 years
bonus_3y.what: Whether bonus shares were issued in the last three years.
bonus_3y.read: After a bonus, compare old prices and dividends only on an adjusted basis.
bonus_3y.why: Your holding's value does not change: the price falls in proportion to the extra shares.
bonus_3y.formula: Yes (1) when a bonus issue has an ex-date in the last three years.

split_3y.label: Stock split in last 3 years
split_3y.what: Whether the shares were split in the last three years.
split_3y.read: Charts and per-share figures must be adjusted for splits to be compared over time.
split_3y.why: It makes shares cheaper to buy in small amounts; the value of your holding stays the same.
split_3y.formula: Yes (1) when a stock split has an ex-date in the last three years.

buyback_3y.label: Buyback in last 3 years
buyback_3y.what: Whether the company bought back shares in the last three years.
buyback_3y.read: A buyback at a high price can destroy value; one at a low price can create it.
buyback_3y.why: It returns cash and raises each remaining shareholder's share of profits.
buyback_3y.formula: Yes (1) when a buyback is recorded in the last three years.

actions_1y.label: Corporate actions in the last year
actions_1y.what: How many corporate actions happened in the last year.
actions_1y.read: FinLit's 'company events' filters let you screen for recent bonuses, splits and buybacks.
actions_1y.why: Corporate actions change prices and share counts, so past figures need adjusting.
actions_1y.formula: Count of dividends, bonus issues, splits and similar events with a date in the last 365 days.

flag_loss.label: Loss-making
flag_loss.what: Whether the company made a loss in the latest year.
flag_loss.read: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.
flag_loss.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
flag_loss.formula: Yes (1) when net profit of the latest year is below zero. Yes (1) or no (0). It is a screener warning sign, not a verdict on the company.

flag_cfo_negative.label: Negative operating cash flow
flag_cfo_negative.what: Whether the business used cash in its operations last year.
flag_cfo_negative.read: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.
flag_cfo_negative.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
flag_cfo_negative.formula: Yes (1) when operating cash flow of the latest year is below zero. Yes (1) or no (0). It is a screener warning sign, not a verdict on the company.

flag_cash_gap.label: Profit not backed by cash
flag_cash_gap.what: Whether less than half of reported profit turned into operating cash.
flag_cash_gap.read: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.
flag_cash_gap.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
flag_cash_gap.formula: Yes (1) when cash conversion (operating cash flow ÷ net profit) is below 50% while profit is positive. Yes (1) or no (0). It is a screener warning sign, not a verdict on the company.

flag_high_debt.label: High debt
flag_high_debt.what: Whether borrowings are more than twice shareholders' equity.
flag_high_debt.read: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.
flag_high_debt.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
flag_high_debt.formula: Yes (1) when debt to equity is above 2. Yes (1) or no (0). It is a screener warning sign, not a verdict on the company. Not applied to banks.

flag_weak_cover.label: Weak interest cover
flag_weak_cover.what: Whether operating profit covers interest less than 1.5 times.
flag_weak_cover.read: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.
flag_weak_cover.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
flag_weak_cover.formula: Yes (1) when interest coverage is below 1.5. Yes (1) or no (0). It is a screener warning sign, not a verdict on the company. Not applied to banks.

flag_profit_fall.label: Profit fell sharply
flag_profit_fall.what: Whether net profit dropped by more than a fifth in the latest year.
flag_profit_fall.read: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.
flag_profit_fall.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
flag_profit_fall.formula: Yes (1) when net profit fell by more than 20% against a positive profit the year before. Yes (1) or no (0). It is a screener warning sign, not a verdict on the company.

flag_promoter_selling.label: Promoters selling
flag_promoter_selling.what: Whether promoters cut their holding by more than 2 points in a year.
flag_promoter_selling.read: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.
flag_promoter_selling.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
flag_promoter_selling.formula: Yes (1) when promoter holding fell by more than 2 percentage points over a year. Yes (1) or no (0). It is a screener warning sign, not a verdict on the company.

flag_below_trend.label: Far below long-term trend
flag_below_trend.what: Whether the price is far under its long-term average.
flag_below_trend.read: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.
flag_below_trend.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
flag_below_trend.formula: Yes (1) when the price is more than 20% below its 200-day exponential moving average. Yes (1) or no (0). It is a screener warning sign, not a verdict on the company.

flag_count.label: Number of red flags
flag_count.what: How many of the eight red-flag checks apply to the company.
flag_count.read: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.
flag_count.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
flag_count.formula: How many of the eight red-flag checks apply; counted only when at least four of the eight could be checked.

is_bank.label: Bank or lender
is_bank.what: Whether the company is a bank or lender, whose accounts follow different rules.
is_bank.read: Judge NBFCs on asset quality, funding costs and capital, like banks.
is_bank.why: NBFCs cannot take ordinary savings deposits, so they depend more on borrowing.
is_bank.formula: Yes (1) when most of the company's income is interest earned, as for a bank or NBFC.

interest_to_revenue.label: Interest cost to income
interest_to_revenue.what: A bank's interest expense as a share of its total income; a FinLit screener filter for lenders.
interest_to_revenue.read: Use it with NIM and CASA to compare lenders' funding strength.
interest_to_revenue.why: Lower means cheaper funding relative to what the bank earns.
interest_to_revenue.formula: Finance costs (interest paid) ÷ total income of the latest year × 100.

volume.label: Volume (latest day)
volume.what: The number of shares traded in a period, usually a day.
volume.read: FinLit's 'volume spike' alert fires when volume is several times its 20-day average.
volume.why: Price moves on high volume carry more weight than moves on thin volume.
volume.formula: Shares traded on the latest trading day.

avg_volume_20d.label: Average volume (20 days)
avg_volume_20d.what: Average volume is the typical daily volume over a window such as 20 days. A spike is a day far above that average.
avg_volume_20d.read: Check filings on spike days to find the reason.
avg_volume_20d.why: A spike often comes with news, results or a large investor buying or selling.
avg_volume_20d.formula: The middle (median) daily volume of the 20 trading days before the latest day, so one block-deal day cannot set the 'usual' level. It is a median, not a mean.

volume_vs_avg.label: Volume against 20-day average
volume_vs_avg.what: Today's volume as a multiple of the usual daily volume.
volume_vs_avg.read: Check filings on spike days to find the reason.
volume_vs_avg.why: A spike often comes with news, results or a large investor buying or selling.
volume_vs_avg.formula: Volume of the latest day ÷ the 20-day median volume.

turnover_cr.label: Traded value (latest day)
turnover_cr.what: Volume multiplied by price: the rupee value of shares traded in a day.
turnover_cr.read: For small investors, a few crore rupees of daily traded value is usually enough; tiny traded values make exits hard.
turnover_cr.why: It is the best measure of how easily a stock can be bought or sold.
turnover_cr.formula: Latest price × latest day's volume ÷ 1 crore, in ₹ crore.

high_52w.label: 52-week high
high_52w.what: The highest and lowest prices of the past year. Position in the range shows where today's price sits between the two.
high_52w.read: Near the 52-week low is not automatically cheap; check whether the business has weakened.
high_52w.why: They frame the recent price history at a glance.
high_52w.formula: The highest price of the last 52 weeks.

low_52w.label: 52-week low
low_52w.what: The highest and lowest prices of the past year. Position in the range shows where today's price sits between the two.
low_52w.read: Near the 52-week low is not automatically cheap; check whether the business has weakened.
low_52w.why: They frame the recent price history at a glance.
low_52w.formula: The lowest price of the last 52 weeks.

pct_from_high.label: Below 52-week high
pct_from_high.what: How far the price is under its 52-week high.
pct_from_high.read: Near the 52-week low is not automatically cheap; check whether the business has weakened.
pct_from_high.why: They frame the recent price history at a glance.

pct_from_low.label: Above 52-week low
pct_from_low.what: How far the price is above its 52-week low.
pct_from_low.read: Near the 52-week low is not automatically cheap; check whether the business has weakened.
pct_from_low.why: They frame the recent price history at a glance.

range_pos.label: Position in 52-week range
range_pos.what: The highest and lowest prices of the past year. Position in the range shows where today's price sits between the two.
range_pos.read: Near the 52-week low is not automatically cheap; check whether the business has weakened.
range_pos.why: They frame the recent price history at a glance.
range_pos.formula: (Price − 52-week low) ÷ (52-week high − 52-week low) × 100. 0 is at the low, 100 at the high.

near_high.label: Near 52-week high
near_high.what: Whether the price is within 3% of its 52-week high.
near_high.read: Near the 52-week low is not automatically cheap; check whether the business has weakened.
near_high.why: They frame the recent price history at a glance.
near_high.formula: Yes (1) when the price is within 3% of the 52-week high.

near_low.label: Near 52-week low
near_low.what: Whether the price is within 3% of its 52-week low.
near_low.read: Near the 52-week low is not automatically cheap; check whether the business has weakened.
near_low.why: They frame the recent price history at a glance.
near_low.formula: Yes (1) when the price is within 3% of the 52-week low.

fno.label: Has futures & options (F&O)
fno.what: Whether the stock has futures and options contracts on NSE.
fno.read: It tells you only that derivatives trade on the stock, not whether the share is good or bad value. Exchanges admit stocks to F&O by size and how much they trade.
fno.why: F&O stocks are among the most traded, and their contracts follow exchange rules such as a fixed lot size.
fno.formula: Yes (1) when NSE stock futures on the company appear in the broker Dhan's daily instrument file, otherwise no (0). Blank when the company is not matched in that file on NSE.

vs_ema50.label: Price against 50-day average
vs_ema50.what: How far the price sits above (+) or below (−) its 50-day exponential moving average.
vs_ema50.read: Price above its 200-day average is often read as a long-term uptrend; below as a downtrend.
vs_ema50.why: It smooths daily noise to show the trend.
vs_ema50.formula: (Price − 50-day exponential moving average) ÷ that average × 100. FinLit uses the exponential average, which weights recent days more.

vs_ema200.label: Price against 200-day average
vs_ema200.what: How far the price sits above (+) or below (−) its 200-day exponential moving average.
vs_ema200.read: Price above its 200-day average is often read as a long-term uptrend; below as a downtrend.
vs_ema200.why: It smooths daily noise to show the trend.
vs_ema200.formula: (Price − 200-day exponential moving average) ÷ that average × 100. FinLit uses the exponential average, which weights recent days more.

vsEma50Pct.label: Price vs 50-day EMA
vsEma50Pct.what: How far the price sits above (+) or below (−) its 50-day exponential moving average.
vsEma50Pct.read: Price above its 200-day average is often read as a long-term uptrend; below as a downtrend.
vsEma50Pct.why: It smooths daily noise to show the trend.

vsEma200Pct.label: Price vs 200-day EMA
vsEma200Pct.what: How far the price sits above (+) or below (−) its 200-day exponential moving average.
vsEma200Pct.read: Price above its 200-day average is often read as a long-term uptrend; below as a downtrend.
vsEma200Pct.why: It smooths daily noise to show the trend.

volatility.label: Volatility (yearly)
volatility.what: How much a price swings up and down, usually measured as the standard deviation of returns and stated per year.
volatility.read: A stock with 21% yearly volatility often moves around 1.3% on a typical day.
volatility.why: Higher volatility means a bumpier ride and more chance of large short-term losses.
volatility.formula: Standard deviation of the last 60 daily returns × √252, shown as a yearly percentage. It reflects the last 60 trading days, not a full year.

max_drawdown.label: Worst fall (since data starts)
max_drawdown.what: The fall from a previous peak to a later low, in percent. FinLit's 'distance from the running high' chart shows it over time.
max_drawdown.read: Ask yourself whether you could hold through the stock's worst past drawdown.
max_drawdown.why: It shows how painful the worst stretches have been.
max_drawdown.formula: The deepest fall from a running peak to a later low in the stored daily price history.

overall.label: Overall score (retired)
overall.what: The retired 0–100 overall score of a company: the average of five pillar scores. FinLit Prism is now FinLit's only company score.
overall.read: It is no longer shown. Read FinLit Prism instead.
overall.why: It turns dozens of numbers into one readable starting point.
overall.formula: The average of the available pillar scores, out of 100. Each input scores 18, 38, 58, 76 or 92 against four fixed thresholds and a pillar is the average of its inputs.

pillar_quality.label: Quality pillar (retired)
pillar_quality.what: A part of the retired overall score, the Quality pillar: returns on capital and how well profit turns into cash.
pillar_quality.read: It is no longer shown. Read FinLit Prism and its parts instead.
pillar_quality.why: A stock can be strong in some pillars and weak in others; the pillars show where.
pillar_quality.formula: Average of the scores for ROE, ROCE and cash conversion (CFO/PAT).

pillar_growth.label: Growth pillar (retired)
pillar_growth.what: A part of the retired overall score, the Growth pillar: how fast sales and profit have grown.
pillar_growth.read: It is no longer shown. Read FinLit Prism and its parts instead.
pillar_growth.why: A stock can be strong in some pillars and weak in others; the pillars show where.
pillar_growth.formula: Average of the scores for sales CAGR, profit CAGR and latest sales growth.

pillar_profitability.label: Profitability pillar (retired)
pillar_profitability.what: A part of the retired overall score, the Profitability pillar: margins and how hard the assets work.
pillar_profitability.read: It is no longer shown. Read FinLit Prism and its parts instead.
pillar_profitability.why: A stock can be strong in some pillars and weak in others; the pillars show where.
pillar_profitability.formula: Average of the scores for operating margin, net margin and asset turnover.

pillar_balance.label: Balance sheet pillar (retired)
pillar_balance.what: A part of the retired overall score, the Balance sheet pillar: how much of the assets are funded by liabilities, and whether profit is backed by cash.
pillar_balance.read: It is no longer shown. Read FinLit Prism and its parts instead.
